newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-U.S. goes from strength to strength.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-U.S. goes from strength to strength.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries are looking consistently attractive compared to their European counterparts, analysts said on Monday.
Expectations of an imminent interest rate rise have receded, supply is drying up and the trading atmosphere seems like an oasis of tranquillity compared with the tumult in Europe.
But with the short end looking over-optimistic, investors should stick to the long end of the curve, analysts said.

"There is no inflation pressure in the States, the dollar is looking cheap. It's very difficult to see what could disturb the relative value of the U.S. over Germany," said David Hewitt, bond strategist at Tokyo Mitsubishi in London.
The 10-year T-note/Bund yield gap was quoted at 85 basis points at 0932 GMT, near the bottom of its recent range after hitting a peak of 122 basis points in April.
The gap snapped in last week on the back of weak retail sales and producer price data, quelling speculation of an interest rate rise at the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting on July 1 and 2.

The market should also be comfortable with the data this week. Consumer prices for May should be benign, indicating an economy running at full tilt with little inflation to eat into bond yields, analysts said.

Meanwhile, European bonds were forging ahead on expectations of a deal at the EU summit in Amsterdam on a key sticking point of European currency union -- making France's desire for jobs creation compatible with Germany's determination to stick to EMU's strict financial conditions.
It appeared a deal on the stability pact, a system of censures and fines designed to stop countries overspending after EMU's planned 1999 launch data, was close at hand.
But Stephen Lewis, chief economist at London Bond Broking, said any lift European bonds might get from a stability pact deal would be fleeting.

"If we get news of an agreement, that really should be a selling signal for traders," he said. "By the time the analysts have pulled apart the implications of the deal I don't think the market will like what it sees. It's very unlikely they will be able to hold this together."

Lewis expects the US/Bund gap to slim down to around 80 basis points in the next few days while Hewitt had a three-month target of 75 basis points. He favoured the 10-year sector where the U.S. government has scrubbed auctions for July and October.
Lewis however, was not as positive on the U.S. economy as some analysts and said stronger data in the second half of the year might catch the market off guard.

"The data last week was good but it reflected what happened in the second quarter when demand came off the boil. What the Fed will be worried about is what happens in the second half of the year," he said.
Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International in London, said the short end of the Treasury curve may have stepped too far into positive territory.
On average, two-year notes yield 65 to 70 basis points over the fed funds target rate when interest rate policy is deemed to be neutral, he said.

"Currently we're only trading 50 basis points over and that's looking very expensive," he said. "If it falls much further the market is beginning to price in a cut in interest rates which seems a leap of logic."
Two-year notes were currently yielding 6.01 percent while the fed funds target rate was at 5.50 percent after a 25 basis point rise on March 25.
The yield on the long bond, however, still had room to slip lower from the current 6.71 percent, he said.

"We broke through 6.75 percent on Friday. The near term target is 6.50 percent and against that background it's outperformance against European markets," he said. --International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6176
